video_caption: The video opens with an animated 3D global view showing Earth's internal structure and plate tectonics. Red convection currents circulate in the mantle, driving a divergent plate boundary where magma rises to form new crust along a red line on the Earth's surface. Above this animated Earth, a brown rectangular banner displays the title "Plate Tectonics & California Geology" (English), followed by "Geoscience Video Tutorial Produced by Katryn Wiese City College of San Francisco" (English). Below the Earth model, a purple box lists the "Plate Tectonics Video Series:" (English) with seven parts, where "Part IV: Plate Tectonics and Calif. Geology" (English) is highlighted by a red rectangle. At 0:09, a yellow rectangular banner with the bold black text "SO WHAT?!?!" (English) slides in, asking about the relevance of plate tectonics. The scene then transitions at 0:14 to a split screen. On the left is a satellite image of the Western United States and Canada, showing the coastline and vast ocean. On the right, a geological map of the same region depicts plate boundaries, faults, and relative plate motions, including the San Andreas Fault and various offshore fracture zones and ridges (e.g., Juan de Fuca Ridge, Mendocino Fracture Zone, Blanco Fracture Zone, subduction zone). At 0:16, a red curved line highlights California on the satellite image, which then morphs into a red oval at 0:17, encircling the state on both the satellite image and the geological map. At 0:25, the red oval on the map disappears as a large red arrow points from the satellite image towards the Mendocino Fracture Zone on the map, then further left across the ocean on the satellite image. At 0:30, a new diagram appears in the top-left, illustrating a cross-section of an oceanic spreading center with magma rising and new crust forming, labeled "PACIFIC PLATE - Juan de Fuca Ridge" (English). Concurrently, a large red arrow on the satellite image points to the offshore spreading center, and another red arrow on the geological map points to the Juan de Fuca Ridge.

The video segment illustrates plate tectonics along the western coast of North America, featuring a convergent plate boundary and a transform fault system. It begins with an animated diagram on the left showing an oceanic plate subducting beneath a continental plate, forming a trench, generating earthquakes, and leading to an "UCA" (Upper Continental Arc) with volcanic eruptions (0:06-0:20). Concurrently, a map on the right displays the geological features of the Pacific Northwest and California, including a "SUBDUCTION ZONE" (Subduction Zone) labeled as the "SOURCE OF GREAT EARTHQUAKES" (Source of Great Earthquakes), with the "PACIFIC PLATE" (Pacific Plate) and "GORDA PLATE" (Gorda Plate) indicated by blue arrows moving east. A large red arrow points inland to the "CASCADE VOLCANIC ARC" (Cascade Volcanic Arc), characterized by pink triangles representing "MAJOR VOLCANOES" (Major Volcanoes) and a "VOLCANIC PLATFORM" (Volcanic Platform). A green oval then circles the entire "CASCADE VOLCANIC ARC" on the map, followed by another green oval highlighting its southern extension in California.

The scene transitions (0:28-0:38) to a satellite view of California on the left, while on the right, images of "Mt. Shasta" (Mount Shasta) and "Lassen Peak" (Lassen Peak) appear, each with a red arrow pointing to its location on the satellite map. A black and white photograph of an explosive eruption of "Lassen Peak" (Lassen Peak) from "May 22nd, 1915" (May 22nd, 1915) is then shown at the bottom left.

The video then shifts (0:38-0:55) to seafloor spreading and transform faults. The satellite view shows oceanic ridges off the coast, and a red arrow points to the "Juan de Fuca ridge" (Juan de Fuca Ridge) on the map. A diagram at the bottom illustrates how transform faults offset spreading ridges. Green ovals highlight the "Juan de Fuca ridge" (Juan de Fuca Ridge) and the "Blanco fracture zone" (Blanco Fracture Zone), demonstrating the offset.

Continuing (0:55-1:14), a red arrow moves south on both the satellite view and the map, tracing the "Mendocino fracture zone" (Mendocino Fracture Zone), which is highlighted by a green oval. The arrow then follows the "San Andreas fault" (San Andreas Fault) through California, depicted with purple arrows showing "Relative motion of North America Plate" (Relative motion of North America Plate) and "Relative motion of Pacific Plate" (Relative motion of Pacific Plate). A red line appears on the satellite map corresponding to the fault. The map zooms in to show the "San Andreas fault" (San Andreas Fault) connecting south to the "East Pacific Rise" (East Pacific Rise) in the Gulf of California, which is also highlighted by a green oval.

Finally (1:14-1:23), the "San Andreas fault" (San Andreas Fault) is highlighted in green on the map, and the red line on the satellite map glows, with text labeling it as the "San Andreas Fault System" (San Andreas Fault System).

The video segment presents a dynamic simulation of the 1989 M6.9 Loma Prieta Earthquake's shaking intensity across the San Francisco Bay Area in California. At the top left of the black screen, the text "1989 M6.9 Loma Prieta Eq" (1989 Magnitude 6.9 Loma Prieta Earthquake) identifies the event. A time counter, displayed as "Time=" followed by a numerical value, increments throughout the segment, starting at "Time= 10.0 s" (Time = 10.0 seconds) and reaching "Time= 66.0 s" (Time = 66.0 seconds) by the end. In the top right corner, a "Shaking Intensity" legend shows Roman numerals I through IX corresponding to a color scale, ranging from blue (lowest intensity) through green and yellow to red (highest intensity). The main visual is a satellite or topographic map of the California coast, centered on the San Francisco Bay, with various cities such as Santa Rosa, Napa, Richmond, Concord, Livermore, San Francisco, Oakland, San Mateo, Palo Alto, Fremont, San Jose, Gilroy, and Santa Cruz labeled in yellow text. Initially, a prominent red and yellow area, indicating the highest shaking intensity, is visible near Santa Cruz, which is the earthquake's epicenter. As the time progresses, this colored area expands outwards from Santa Cruz. The most intense red and yellow shaking remains concentrated near the epicenter, while concentric rings of green and blue, representing decreasing shaking intensity, spread across the entire Bay Area, covering San Francisco, Oakland, San Jose, and other cities, visually demonstrating the propagation of seismic waves and their impact over time and distance. The "USGS" logo is visible in the bottom left corner of the screen.

The video segment begins with a "REVIEW TIME" slide featuring three multiple-choice geology questions about plate boundaries and the San Andreas Fault. A yellow box on the left displays "PAUSE NOW" and a countdown message that first states, "You have 7 seconds before the answers appear, so pause now!" (0:05) and then changes to "You have 5 seconds before the answers disappear, so pause now!" (0:07). The correct answers are highlighted in red boxes: "e. Transform" for the first two questions, and "d. 25 million years" for the third. At 0:12, the scene transitions to an animated geological map of the western United States, displaying the Pacific Plate, the North American Plate, and the subducting Farallon Plate, with red lines indicating plate boundaries and white arrows showing plate movement. An inset diagram in the upper left illustrates a subduction zone, where oceanic crust subducts under continental crust, leading to volcanic activity and granite formation. As the Farallon Plate subducts, a yellow question mark appears on the map, highlighting the area where a spreading center would have been, and a green double-headed arrow indicates an area of crustal tension. At 0:35, the video switches to a satellite image of the western US focusing on the "Basin and Range" province, where a large green double-headed arrow signifies crustal stretching. Below the map, a geological cross-section illustrates how normal faults form parallel mountain ranges and basins due to this stretching, with a red arrow pointing from the map to the "Sierra Nevada" range and another identical red arrow on the cross-section indicating an uplifted block at the western edge. At 0:56, a woman in a light blue shirt and brown pants is shown hiking through a glaciated, rocky mountain landscape with a lake, identified as "Vogelsang, Yosemite." An inset diagram during this scene shows "Granite" forming from "Granitic Magma" deep underground, representing the frozen remnants of old volcanic cores. The video briefly returns to the satellite map at 1:04, reiterating the location of the Sierra Nevada and the Basin and Range stretching with the red and green arrows.

The video segment opens with a satellite image of the western United States, showing the Pacific Ocean to the left and a terrestrial landscape to the right. A red arrow points from the ocean towards the land, labeled "Sierra Nevada," while a green double-headed arrow spans the terrestrial region, labeled "Basin and Range," indicating extension. Below this, a geological cross-section illustrates subduction on the left (west) and rifting on the right (east) with an upward-pointing red arrow indicating mantle melting and rising magma, and a yellow oval highlighting a magma chamber and associated faulting. The scene then transitions to an aerial photo of Mammoth Mountain, nestled among trees and a lake, with text "Mammoth Mountain" and "Areas of dead and dying trees" indicating CO2 emission. The geological cross-section remains, with the red arrow continuing to point upwards into a large magma chamber. A blue circle highlights the location of Mammoth Mountain on the satellite image. The cross-section then expands to a more detailed view of the "Long Valley caldera," showing various geological layers like "bishop tuff," "basement," "congealed magma," and "partially molten magma," with "basalt injections" from below. A blue bracket outlines the caldera, which contains a "resurgent dome" and "postcaldera lavas and fill." The red arrow still points to the deep mantle, now also showing basalt injections. Next, a close-up image of a massive light-colored rock formation appears, labeled "Bishop Tuff: produced from 760,000 year-old eruption." A small inset map of the Western U.S. displays concentric yellow circles originating from "Long Valley Caldera," showing the "Distribution of Bishop Ash in Western U.S.," with distance markers in kilometers. The video then reverts to the Mammoth Mountain aerial photo and the Long Valley cross-section, with green arrows now tracing gas emissions (CO2) from the magma chamber to the surface, affecting the "Areas of dead and dying trees." Finally, the segment transitions to a detailed topographic map of the "Long Valley Caldera" area, with numerous labeled features such as Mono Lake, Panum Crater, Mammoth Mtn., and Hot Creek, along with roads and other geographical points. A blue circle outlines the caldera boundary and the resurgent dome, and a green box highlights the more recent eruption sites like Panum Crater and the Inyo Craters.

The video opens with a split screen: the top-left shows a hiker with a large red backpack and two trekking poles, standing on a rocky outcrop overlooking a mountainous landscape with a prominent peak labeled "Cathedral Peaks, Yosemite." Below this, a geological cross-section diagram illustrates a volcano erupting, with molten rock underground labeled "Granitic Magma" and solid rock above labeled "Granite." On the right, a "Geologic Map of California" is displayed, with a legend and various colors, and text overlaying it states "RED = Ancient Sierra Granite" (English). As the narrator speaks about the San Andreas Fault, a green line appears on the map, representing the "San Andreas Fault System" (English), with blue arrows indicating the relative motion of the plates. Red circular highlights move along the green fault line, indicating areas where granite has been displaced. The scene transitions to a zoomed-in view of the San Francisco Bay Area on the same map, with "180 miles" (English) marked as a scale. Red arrows and text labels point to "Pt. Reyes Granite" (English) and "Montara Mountain Granite" (English), indicating locations of granite. A satellite view appears on the left, showing a green line labeled "San Andreas Fault" (English) cutting through a landscape, with a red arrow pointing to a mountain labeled "Montara Mountain" (English) and a yellow "S" indicating south. The video then transitions to a "REVIEW TIME" (English) slide with three multiple-choice questions about plate boundaries and California volcanism. A yellow "PAUSE NOW" (English) box appears on the left, with text "You have 7 seconds before the answers appear, so pause now!" (English). After a few seconds, a red box highlights "e. Transform" (English) for the first question, "c. Convergent (continent-ocean)" (English) for the second question, and "a. Sierran granites were formed from the same style of subduction that produces today's Cascade Mountains." (English) and "b. The volcanoes that produced Sierran granites went extinct tens of millions of years ago and have long since eroded away." (English) for the third question. The yellow box now says "You have 5 seconds before the answers disappear, so pause now!" (English).

The video begins at 0:05 with a man in a light grey hoodie, dark shorts, and a baseball cap standing with his arms outstretched at the base of a very steep, layered rock cliff. The cliff face shows distinct geological folds and strata, with patches of green vegetation. In the upper right corner, a white text box with red lettering reads, "Devil's Slide: sediments deposited with changing sea levels along the coast." At 0:09, the scene transitions to an animated 3D geological cross-section diagram on the left, depicting an oceanic plate subducting beneath a continental plate, with a mountain range and a volcano on the continental side. Red arrows illustrate the plate movement. Concurrently, on the right, a spinning globe of Earth shows continents and oceans, with plate boundaries marked by red lines, and a text overlay indicating geological time: "80 Ma" (80 million years ago). As the animation progresses, colored blocks (red, yellow, purple) representing terranes are shown moving towards the subduction zone and being accreted (scraped off and added) to the continental margin, which gradually expands westward. The time on the globe updates to "70 Ma," "60 Ma," "50 Ma," and "40 Ma" as these events unfold. At 0:22, the right side of the screen displays a 2D map of the western United States, including Oregon, California, Nevada, and Idaho, with a title "DOCKING TERRANES ON NORTH AMERICAN MARGIN." This map illustrates the "Smartville Terrane" and the "Franciscan subduction zone" along the California coast, along with historical western edges of the North American continent at "225 Ma" and "175 Ma," and a "Suture Zone," demonstrating the accretionary process over geological time. From 0:39, the animated cross-section diagram fills the entire screen, now labeled with various geological features: "Basalt," "Ocean Sediment," "Gabbro," "Serpentinite," "Continental Sediment," "Granite," "Franciscan Complex," "Lithosphere," "Asthenosphere," "Upper Mantle," and "Granitic Magma." A blue rectangular highlight appears sequentially over "Ocean Sediment," then "Continental Sediment," "Serpentinite," and a portion of the "Lithosphere," before finally highlighting the entire subducting oceanic plate, with a black arrow indicating its downward and rightward movement.

The video opens with a split screen displaying four geological scenes from California: a black-and-white image of a barren landscape with "Mt Lassen" (Mount Lassen) text overlay and a large rock in the foreground, a photograph of earthquake damage to a building with "Loma Prieta Damage" text overlay, a colorful stream winding through a valley with mountains in the background labeled "Hot Creek Long Valley", and a close-up of a rock formation in the bottom left, partially obscured by the word "June". A voiceover discusses California's landscape and major geological hazards. The scene transitions to a satellite view of California on the left and a geological map on the right, showing various plate boundaries and landmass types, including the Juan de Fuca Plate, Cascadia Trench, San Andreas Fault, Guerrero Terrane, and Salton Trough, with a legend explaining terms like "Island arc," "Convergent boundary," and "Transform boundary." The voiceover explains how landmasses have combined to form California. Next, the screen shows a group of people examining a steep, rocky, brown hillside, with the text "Accreted Terrane: Ocean Sediment (Chert) Marin Headlands" at the bottom left. An inset picture appears on the right, showing another group of people on a rocky beach with waves crashing against a mountainous coast, labeled "Montara Granite Gray Whale Cove Beach." Later, a second inset appears on the top left of the main image, showing people sitting on rocks in a rugged coastal area, with the text "Accreted Terrane: Continental Sands Baker Beach." The voiceover encourages viewers to explore these locations. The video then transitions to a "REVIEW TIME" slide with two multiple-choice questions on a white background, and a yellow sidebar labeled "PAUSE NOW" indicating a countdown for answers. Question 1 asks: "Which of the following plate boundaries does NOT exist currently in or near California?" with options a-e (Convergent (continent-continent), Convergent (ocean-ocean), Convergent (continent-ocean), Divergent, Transform). Question 2 asks: "Which of the following material comprises California? (Choose all that apply.)" with options a-c (Accreted terranes from ocean subduction, Sedimentary deposits formed in basins along the coast as sea level has risen and fallen, Volcanic rock erupted from current and previously active volcanoes). After a few seconds, red boxes highlight options a and b for Question 1, and options a, b, and c for Question 2 as the correct answers, and the yellow sidebar changes to "You have 5 seconds before the answers disappear, so pause now!". Finally, a credit screen appears with "Plate Tectonics and California Geology," producer and institution details, copyright information (Creative Commons Attribution – Noncommercial – Share Alike 3.0), and a list of image and animation sources. On the right, a "Plate Tectonics Video Series" list is shown with a red arrow pointing to "Part V: Hotspots" as "Next up," and a small image of the beach field trip at the bottom. The source list expands to include more detailed credits. The video concludes with a final credit screen featuring a film camera icon and "Open Education Geoscience Resource," acknowledging National Science Foundation support and Creative Commons licensing.
